lesson.title: Fire and Forget: Why UDP Trades Reliability for Speed
lesson.summary: UDP is a minimal, connectionless transport layer protocol that sends data without setup, acknowledgment, or retry, trading reliability for the lowest possible overhead and latency.
lesson.body:
UDP is one of the two foundational transport layer protocols, and like every transport layer protocol its basic job is to get data from a process on one host to a process on another, using port numbers to sort out which application on the receiving machine should get the data. Where UDP stands apart is in how little else it does. It is defined in RFC 768, published in 1980, one of the shortest and oldest RFCs still in everyday use, and its brevity is not an accident, it reflects a protocol that was deliberately designed to do very little on purpose.

UDP is connectionless, which means there is no handshake before data flows and no persistent state kept about the conversation on either end. Each datagram a process sends is handled entirely on its own, addressed by source and destination IP and port, with no promise that it will arrive, that it will arrive only once, or that it will arrive in the order it was sent. Nothing tracks whether a previous datagram made it through before the next one is sent. That absence of bookkeeping is precisely the point: it keeps per packet overhead and latency as low as the underlying network allows.

That minimalism shows up directly in the header, which is only 8 bytes: a source port, a destination port, a length field, and a checksum, each 16 bits. Compare that to what is missing, there is no sequence number, no acknowledgment number, no window field, no retransmission timer, nothing that would require either side to remember anything about the datagrams that came before. The entire tradeoff UDP makes is visible in that one small header.

That tradeoff is worth it whenever an application cares more about freshness than completeness. A DNS query is a single small request and a single small response, and if the response is lost it is cheaper to just resend the query than to pay for a stateful connection setup for one round trip. A live voice or video call has no use for a late audio frame, since by the time a retransmission would arrive the moment it belonged to has already passed, so it is better to skip it and move on. Online games favor the most current position update over a perfectly complete history of old ones. Applications that do need some reliability on top of UDP are free to build it themselves, tailored to exactly what they need, which is part of why newer protocols like QUIC are built on top of UDP rather than on top of TCP.

A simple example makes the tradeoff concrete: a DNS resolver sends a single UDP datagram to port 53 asking for the address of a domain, and the server replies with a single UDP datagram back. There is no connection setup cost paid before that exchange, and if the reply happens to be lost, the resolver notices only because no answer showed up in time, and it simply sends the same query again.
